We just published a list of the 10 Best AI Stocks to Buy After Wells Fargo's Outlook Upgrade and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) ranked 6th on this list. Wells Fargo is no longer telling investors to stay away from the AI infrastructure trade. In a new note, analysts led by Ohsung Kwon raised the firm's view on US AI infrastructure to neutral from negative. The change follows a deep selloff. Semiconductor shares trade about 38% below their June highs, and the multiples investors pay for them have compressed. At current prices, the analysts said, valuations imply earnings growth of only about 8% a year. A compressed multiple means investors now pay less for each dollar of expected profit. That can happen even while earnings keep rising, which is why a stock can fall while its business improves. Democratic wins in the midterm elections, including in states that oppose new data centers, fueled concerns about regulation. A stricter permitting climate could slow construction and raise its cost, which would cut into the spending that has fed AI company revenue. The selloff has erased about $3 trillion from the S&P 500. Readers following the pullback can find the names analysts like most in our list of oversold AI stocks with 50%-plus upside. Kwon and his team said the risk-reward is now reasonable after the drop. AI spending added about 8 percentage points to S&P 500 earnings growth over the past year. The Wells Fargo analysts wrote that "The tailwind is expected to continue in 2027," and that it largely disappears in 2028 as spending growth slows and depreciation costs rise. Depreciation explains much of the concern. Companies spread the cost of data centers and chips over several years, so those charges keep landing on income statements even after the buying slows. Those charges are real expenses even though the cash left the company earlier. Profit growth then shrinks, just as the spending that lifted it fades. Analysts build their forecasts from spending levels, so a plateau in budgets changes the math quickly. The bigger risk, the analysts said, is a downturn in earnings per share once capital spending peaks. They also pointed to extra supply arriving in 2028 that prices do not yet reflect. For investors, the question is how much of that is already in share prices after the drop. Companies still growing quickly through the selloff are the subject of our roundup of the fastest-growing AI stocks. The Wells Fargo shift is a move from caution to a neutral stance, not a call that the selloff is over. Nvidia made it to our list because it has an average upside potential of 83%. Baird downgraded Nvidia to Neutral from Outperform on November 11 and cut its target to $200 from $500, pointing to the outlook for AI spending and risks tied to China. Evercore ISI followed on November 12, moving the stock to In Line from Outperform with a $186 target. Oppenheimer also lowered its rating that day, to Perform from Outperform. Nvidia designs the processors that train and run most AI models, so any doubt about customer spending lands on it first. Its chips sit in the data centers of the largest cloud companies, the same buyers whose budgets Baird questions. Investors get a fresh read next Tuesday after the close, when the company reports quarterly results. Wall Street expects earnings of $2.47 per share for the quarter that ended in October. Bulls argue that the stock's slide has left it cheap against its own growth record, while bears, Baird among them, want proof that spending stays strong into next year. Our piece on whether Nvidia's valuation already prices in a growth stall covers the other side of that debate. The report will show whether customers are still placing orders at the same pace. Jensen Huang is out. Jonathan Rose is buying Nvidia stock. Here's why four investing experts see different paths ahead for the AI chip giant. Listen to the audio version of this article (generated by AI). NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) is facing a new test after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a personal-conduct scandal and national-security questions. For shareholders, the immediate issue is whether the leadership shakeup changes the company’s earnings outlook, competitive position or the price investors are willing to pay for its growth. Jonathan Rose isn’t waiting for the dust to settle. During his November 12 Masters in Trading: LIVE, Jonathan said: “I am buying Nvidia right now.” He said he bought shares that morning and was bullish at prevailing prices. Later in the session, he said he had increased his personal position by roughly 20% to 25%. Our analysts aren’t all making the same call, and that’s useful. Jonathan is buying. Louis Navellier is holding and waiting for earnings. Luke Lango is watching how Nvidia’s competitive position evolves, while Eric Fry is asking whether investors will still pay the same premium for its growth. We’ll take a closer look at each of their views, but first, here’s how the scandal unfolded. What started as a personal scandal quickly became a much bigger problem for Nvidia. On November 8, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO, admitted he’d been unfaithful to his wife. According to The New York Times, the woman was Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese citizen and executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected Alice Huang of gathering information for Beijing. Megaspeed had also faced scrutiny over whether advanced Nvidia chips were being diverted to China in violation of U.S. export restrictions. That raised an uncomfortable question: Could sensitive information have fallen into the wrong hands? Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation, and Jensen publicly apologized to his family, employees and shareholders. On November 11, The New York Times reported a second alleged relationship, this time with Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reported to Jensen. By November 12, Jensen had resigned, and longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress had been named interim CEO. To be clear, the allegations involving Chinese intelligence remain unproven publicly, and there’s no established finding that Jensen compromised confidential information. But investors now face a very real question: Can Nvidia maintain its dominance in AI chips without the man who helped build it? The answer depends on more than who occupies the CEO’s office. Nvidia’s earnings power, its competitive position and investor confidence will all help determine what comes next. And as the latest commentary from our analysts Jonathan, Louis, Luke and Eric shows, there are different ways to assess Nvidia’s prospects from here. Jonathan made that distinction in his November 12 Masters in Trading: LIVE. He called the leadership crisis “a Jensen problem,” and he sees the selloff as a buying opportunity. Jonathan’s bullish case rests on the company’s existing business and the market’s reaction. Nvidia’s chips remain deeply embedded in customers’ computing systems, he argued, and changing suppliers takes years. He believes the stock has become inexpensive following the selloff and that investors may be discounting the company too heavily for the uncertainty around its former CEO. His preferred way to express that view is important. Jonathan favors buying Nvidia shares rather than purchasing upside call options ahead of earnings. During the same session, he noted that Nvidia options were pricing in a roughly 12% move around the upcoming earnings report, a level he considered expensive given that the stock had exceeded that threshold only once in its previous 12 earnings reports. Jonathan knows the next earnings report could change the conversation, and he expects earnings and guidance to drive the stock’s next move. Louis isn’t letting the headlines drive his investment decisions. Before Jensen resigned, Louis discussed the unfolding scandal on Market Buzz and initially believed Nvidia’s board and the U.S. government would eventually clear Jensen of wrongdoing. His departure caught Louis by surprise, but it hasn’t shaken his confidence in Nvidia’s underlying business. For Louis, the earnings story still matters more than the headlines. Before the scandal, analysts were forecasting about 91% sales growth and 90% earnings growth for Nvidia’s third quarter. Those were the expectations Louis cited when explaining why he believes the company’s earnings power remains intact. Nvidia still has its technology, its customers and enormous demand for the chips powering the AI boom. But Louis wants to see how the leadership shakeup affects the company’s outlook. He’s particularly interested in Nvidia’s November 17 earnings report, management’s guidance and whether Wall Street analysts begin lowering their estimates. For now, Louis is holding his Nvidia shares, rather than buying more or selling in response to the scandal. There’s another reason he’s being selective. Louis believes the stock market was already rotating away from some of its familiar technology leaders before Jensen’s resignation. He sees opportunities emerging in other sectors, including energy and healthcare, where his quantitative system is identifying companies with strong earnings prospects. His approach comes down to a simple principle: Follow the sales and earnings, not the headlines. Is Nvidia still one of the best stocks to own, or are stronger opportunities emerging elsewhere? Louis follows the earnings to identify stocks with the greatest potential. Get his free stock picks and daily market insights with the Market 360 e-letter. Sign up for free here. Luke expects AI demand to survive Jensen’s exit. His question is how much of that demand Nvidia will capture. Luke has been making the case that the AI trade could broaden beyond Nvidia. He argues that Jensen’s departure may make it easier for major customers to consider other chip suppliers. He sees that as a competitive risk for Nvidia, even as overall AI spending keeps growing. He sees potential openings for Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD) and custom AI chips, including those supported by Broadcom Inc. (AVGO). Nvidia can remain a major winner in a growing market while facing more competition on price and share. That’s the possibility Luke wants investors to watch. None of that means customers can replace Nvidia overnight. Its installed technology and product roadmap still matter. Luke’s longer-term thesis needs evidence, particularly signs that large buyers are shifting spending to competing platforms. Could Nvidia’s troubles create opportunities elsewhere in AI? Luke follows the companies and technologies that could benefit as the AI market evolves. Get his insights and free stock picks through his Hypergrowth Investing e-letter. Sign up for free. In his November 11 issue of Smart Money, published before Jensen resigned, Eric looked at a risk that can be easy to miss when a company is growing quickly: the stock’s valuation. Even if Nvidia keeps delivering strong sales and earnings, its shares could struggle if investors decide to pay a lower multiple for those profits. Eric sees governance questions, regulatory scrutiny and rising competition as possible reasons that confidence could shift. Eric also noted that some competing chip stocks gained during part of Nvidia’s earlier decline. He cautioned that a few days of trading don’t prove Nvidia has lost customers. That would have to show up in orders, spending and earnings. His point is that a great business and a great stock aren’t always the same thing at every price. Is Nvidia’s stock still worth the price? Any new information about the investigation could also affect confidence. Jonathan has already made his move. Louis wants the earnings and guidance in hand. Nvidia (NVDA) stock would likely take a sharp initial hit if CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, but I believe the long-term investment case would remain intact. Huang has led Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, making his leadership central to the chipmaker's identity and success. Its board is now investigating reports that he was the target of a Chinese intelligence effort. Management has never shared a clear succession plan on who would take over if Huang left, but I'm still bullish on NVDA. The probe hasn't touched the enormous demand for these chips so far, and the stock seems to be priced as if the worst case has happened. As investors and spectators would expect, this probe goes straight to the top. On November 8, the board said a committee of independent directors would run the review with outside counsel. It added that it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised. Huang is cooperating and stays on as CEO for now, a welcome update from those who have been following the company closely and appreciate the significant role that Huang has played in the development of the sector, and of course the company. Get 75% Off TipRanks Premium and unlock powerful investing tools to make smarter, more confident investment decisions Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks At the center of the alleged scandal is Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer based in Singapore. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials believe she was a Chinese intelligence asset, and that Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over two years. Huang then admitted to a personal relationship with her in a note to staff. Beijing has naturally called the spying claims smears. Of course, this story became highly political almost immediately, and most of Washington isn't letting it go. Three House committee chairs want Huang at a closed-door briefing on November 18, one day after earnings. Committee chair Brian Mast is reportedly weighing a subpoena if Huang says no. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has also backed limits on chip sales to China in the annual defense bill. Thinking about all of this as a potential investor, Nvidia has surprisingly never named a successor or explained how it would pick one. Semafor found that the word "succession" doesn't appear once in Nvidia's latest annual report. Microsoft (MSFT) uses it 25 times and Alphabet (GOOGL) uses it 16 times. Huang also has more than 50 people reporting directly to him, so there's no obvious number two to step up, with the exception of some family members perhaps. To me, that's a very deliberate move. Huang has said on occasion that planning around a small, hand-picked group of heirs is toxic, and he'd rather grow a wider group of leaders across the company. Asked in January 2026 how long he'd stay, his answer was "for as long as I deserve it." It's worked pretty well so far for shareholders. However, it also leaves the board without a ready answer if it suddenly needs one. Some analysts are now putting a number on that gap. Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less if Huang were removed. Bernstein downgraded the stock to Outperform with a $200 price target. The names floated as potential stand-ins, such as CFO Colette Kress and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, come from media speculation, not from anything the board has actually said. These feel like safe hands to me, but the sheer power of leadership Huang has demonstrated would be almost impossible to match. Meanwhile, the business momentum Nvidia carried into the fall remains hard to ignore. Q2 Fiscal 2027 revenue rose 106% year-over-year to $96.2 billion. Data center sales climbed 117% to $89 billion, and gross margins held at 75%. For Q3, management guided to about $108 billion in revenue, give or take 2%. That outlook notably assumes zero data center compute sales to China. CFO Colette Kress has also said she expects 70% revenue growth in FY28. If Nvidia hits its guide on November 17, the conversation should shift back to demand, at least for a while. Wednesday gave a hint of that. Shares jumped about 5% in early trading after AI cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV) raised its outlook, which is a reminder that Nvidia's biggest customers are still spending. Even so, the stock is still down about 15% in November. Much of the slide started before the probe, with the stock losing roughly 22% to 24% from its early-October peak through the post-midterm chip sell-off. I would tend to think that a fair amount of the leadership risk is already baked in after such a heavy news event. Nvidia trades at about 21x trailing earnings. On a forward basis, some analysts put the stock at 18.65x. The semiconductor industry's median forward P/E is close to 20.31x, so Nvidia trades at a modest discount of roughly 8% to its peers. Against its own history, the gap is much wider. At 18.65x, the stock is valued at less than half its five-year average of 41.38x, even after more than doubling its sales last quarter. So what's the company worth without its charismatic CEO? At 18.65x, the market is assuming forward earnings of about $9.32 per share. Some analysts speculate that Nvidia without Huang might trade at 10x to 12x, which, by my calculations, comes to roughly $93 to $112. Knock 25% to 30% off today's price, as Ives suggests, and you land at roughly $122 to $130, which is a milder downside than the multiple-compression case. If the board clears Huang and the multiple drifts back toward the sector median of 20.31x, the numbers point to around $189. I'd take that trade, as long as earnings estimates hold up. However, not everyone agrees: Baird cut NVDA to Hold with a $200 target on November 11, and Citi (C) trimmed its target to $225. Wall Street is still firmly behind Nvidia, though the support has thinned slightly this week. NVDA has a Strong Buy consensus based on 29 Buys and seven Holds over the past three months. The average NVDA price target of $290.90 implies 67.44% upside from the last price. For 33 years, Nvidia and Huang have been almost synonymous, and this probe makes it understandable for investors to picture one without the other. With no clear successor, I'd expect a pretty sharp drop if he were forced out. However, the business itself still looks strong, and the shares already trade well below their own history and the sector. I see the current price as a fair entry for long-term investors willing to sit through some near-term noise. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

With Jensen Huang out as CEO at Nvidia (NVDA) and CFO Colette Kress taking on the role of interim CEO, Wall Street, the company's partners, and its customers are waiting to find out who the next permanent CEO will be. There are a number of candidates inside and outside of the company who could fill the position. But prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket have zeroed in on Nvidia VP of hyperscale and high-performance computing Ian Buck as the company's next leader. Both sites rank the odds of Buck taking over at roughly 40%. Buck has worked at Nvidia for the last 22 years, rising from a systems engineer to his current role as the head of the company's biggest businesses. The executive also has the kind of engineering chops that Nvidia's board may find compelling for the CEO role. Buck has a Ph.D. from Stanford University in computer science and, more importantly, developed Nvidia's CUDA technology. CUDA allows companies to use the chip giant's graphics processing units (GPUs) for general computing, a capability that was instrumental in turning Nvidia into the AI powerhouse it is today. But Buck has a hard act to follow. Huang's charismatic personality drew customers and investors, turning him into one of the tech industry's biggest stars. And his penchant for elaborate keynotes at massive venues, where he regularly offered technical deep dives, drew thousands of attendees. It's unclear if any other executive could check all of the same boxes. For now, Wall Street analysts see Kress as a steady hand to guide Nvidia through the current storm. KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst John Vinh wrote in a note to investors that Kress's appointment as interim CEO is constructive "given her tenure as CFO since 2013 and deep institutional knowledge of Nvidia's business and strategy." Whoever Nvidia's board eventually chooses to lead the company will have plenty of questions to answer about its future and whether it can continue to dominate the industry as it did under Huang. Nvidia (NVDA) stock went into free fall Thursday as CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, and retail investors were there to catch it. The question now is whether they bought the bottom or just the first leg down. Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO after reports of two affairs, and CFO Colette Kress is stepping in as interim CEO. The stock fell as much as 14% at the open to its lowest level since June 2025, then clawed back nearly three-quarters of it to close down about 4%. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday with no permanent CEO in sight. Small investors bought a net $111 million of Nvidia stock in the first 30 minutes of trading. According to Vanda Research, that was the stock's biggest opening on record and more than 40 times a normal start. Nvidia has soaked up 61% of all retail buying in US stocks and ETFs this week. Money also poured into leveraged funds betting on Nvidia gains, while funds betting against it drew nothing. "This is very much a one-way flow story for retail," Vanda wrote. Mike Zaccardi, a CFA and CMT, called it "one of the more epic 'buy the news' events in history" on X. The stock briefly slipped below $153, the level that capped it from late 2024 until last June. Then it snapped back on its heaviest trading in more than a year. An old ceiling turning into a floor is a classic sign that buyers are stepping in, and it gives traders a clear line in the sand. A break below Thursday's low would undo the setup. The stock also looks beaten down. Its readings on momentum — a gauge of how fast it's moving — are deeply oversold on a daily chart and nearly so on a weekly one. Nvidia stock is on track for its worst month since September 2022. "Getting close to capitulation in $NVDA," Brian Shannon, founder of Alphatrends, posted on X. Shannon's rule of thumb is to wait for a close back above the stock's five-day moving average, around $175, before trusting a rebound. At its low, Nvidia was down 38% from its October record, nearly as deep as its COVID and tariff crashes. Both of those bounced back to new records within three months. The 2018 and 2022 slides ran deeper and took seven to 14 months. Days like Thursday have mostly paid off. Thursday was the seventh session since 2010 in which Nvidia fell at least 10% and recovered at least half of the drop by the close. The stock was higher a year later after five of the first six. The exception was January 2022, the start of a much deeper sell-off. Wall Street isn't bailing either. Rosenblatt's Kevin Cassidy kept his Buy rating, writing that "we expect employees, suppliers and customers to rally around the company." Goldman Sachs' James Schneider also stuck with a Buy, calling Huang's exit a "meaningful, but measured negative for the stock." That's the catch. Huang was the vision behind Nvidia's biggest bets, including the Bank of Nvidia deals that help fund its own customers. "You defend a stock price because you're kind of betting on that operator to have that vision," Unconventional AI CEO Naveen Rao said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday. Not everyone is ready to call a bottom, though. DoubleLine Capital CEO Jeffrey Gundlach said at the same event he would wait for real panic. Apple offers a historical comparison. When Steve Jobs resigned as CEO on August 24, 2011, Apple shares fell 5.9% in after-hours trading. Tim Cook took over, and the company continued to grow. Abrupt CEO exits at index-heavyweight names have historically split into two cases: departures framed as health or scandal, which tend to be sold first and questioned later, and planned successions with an internal heir, which the tape usually absorbs within sessions. An interim appointment from the CFO chair sits between those poles: it preserves operational continuity but leaves strategy, capital allocation and key customer relationships in limbo, and episodes of this kind have tended to keep the stock trading on succession headlines until a permanent hire is named. The unusual feature here is the cluster of downgrades landing immediately before the announcement, a sequence that will draw scrutiny of who knew what and when, and of any follow-through from regulators or the board. The established second-order pattern in semis is the sympathy rotation: closest GPU rival and custom-silicon beneficiaries have tended to gap on leadership-vacuum logic, though historically that relative trade fades faster than the absolute move in the affected name. Worth noting is the backdrop, claims still consistent with a low-hire, low-fire labour market and a heavy slate of Fed speakers after a hawkish dissenter signalled resistance to larger moves, which keeps the macro bid under the index even as its largest constituent drags. Near-term tells are any interim-CEO communication cadence, board commentary on timeline, and whether customers or hyperscalers signal order hesitation, the channel through which past semi leadership shocks have done lasting rather than cosmetic damage. Nvidia (NVDA) CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO after Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of an affair with a Chinese spy and a company executive. Kress, one of Nvidia's more prominent executives, joined the company in 2013 and helped guide its financial success, transforming it from a video game company into the AI juggernaut it is today. In a statement, Kress said she is committed to building on the work Jensen has done to turn Nvidia into the company it has become. "We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," she said. Kress regularly provides financial updates during Nvidia's quarterly earnings call, making her well-known among analysts and investors. Prior to joining the company, Kress served as senior vice president and CFO for Cisco's (CSCO) Business Technology and Operations Finance group, according to her Nvidia biography. Before joining Cisco, she held positions at Microsoft (MSFT) for 13 years, including as CFO of the company's Server and Tools group. She also worked at Texas Instruments (TXN) in several roles. "Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position," newly appointed Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said in a statement. "She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," he added. Kress succeeds Huang, who is embroiled in two alleged affairs: one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. On Sunday, Huang issued a statement admitting to the initial affair, apologizing to his family and Nvidia employees. According to reports, the woman Huang was seeing, Alice Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based technology firm MegaSpeed and was allegedly acting as a spy on behalf of the Chinese government. Nvidia's board has said it has launched an independent investigation into the matter, but added it has no reason to believe Nvidia trade secrets or national security were compromised. The shock resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday renewed pressure on the chipmaker's shares, with the company shedding almost $500 billion in value since the close of U.S. trading last week. Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Thursday morning. In a statement, the company said Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO. Nvidia shares fell $7.54, or 4.3%, to $166.19, paring its losses after tumbling as much as 14.3% earlier in the day. The latest drop comes after the stock shed 9.6% of its value in trading on Monday and Tuesday following the disclosure last weekend that Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset. Nvidia, co-founded by Huang in 1993, became a key player in artificial intelligence due to its powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms. Because of Nvidia's importance to the growing industry, its chips are subject to export controls that limit their sales to China. Huang had pushed the Trump administration to relax some of those regulations. Huang, one of the world's best-known CEOs, has served as the face of the AI industry, promoting its benefits and arguing that new regulations weren't necessary to ensure its safety. Before this week's revelations about his relationship with Chinese business executive Alice Huang (no relation), he had been seen as essential to Nvidia's success, with Wall Street analysts warning that the stock could plunge if he were ousted or resigned. Separately, The New York Times reported Thursday that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, citing other company employees. Huang's "value to the company pre and post this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia," said Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives in a Thursday research note. In a separate report, Ives estimated Nvidia's value at $225 per share if Huang left the company, compared with $300 per share if he remained at the helm. "There is no credible way to put a precise revenue loss on his departure," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. "Customers buy Nvidia's computing power, software and networking ecosystem, and those advantages wouldn't disappear with its CEO," she said. Nvidia's woes also come at a sensitive time for the AI industry, which has already faced investor concerns about a potential slowdown. Among the questions facing the sector is whether it will prove profitable enough to justify massive investments in the technology. Anthropic's initial public offering will provide another key test, with the Claude AI bot developer expected to make its market debut as early as next week. title: NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition - NVIDIA Newsroom
content:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately. Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates. Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft. The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys. “Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” “NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry. NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT. title: AMD Has Opportunity As NVDA Faces Scrutiny And Potential Leadership Vacuum, William Blair Says — Sees Runway For Shares - TradingView
content: Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) was upgraded by William Blair on Thursday, with the brokerage citing an improving risk/reward outlook as its biggest AI chip rival, Nvidia (NVDA), faces leadership uncertainty. The upgrade comes amid growing uncertainty at Nvidia following reports of CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia’s board is meeting to discuss Huang’s possible removal, raising questions about the chipmaker's leadership succession. According to a note cited by TheFly, William Blair upgraded AMD to ‘Outperform’ from ‘Market Perform,’ saying the stock has room to rise as Nvidia faces scrutiny and a leadership vacuum, while AMD’s competitive position improves and its valuation looks attractive. At the time of writing in premarket trading, stocktwits.com/symbol/AMDAMD stock was up 3% while NVDA stock was down nearly 7%. William Blair said all four factors behind its previous rating have shifted in AMD’s favor since it initiated coverage in July. Intel's (INTC) Xeon server processor roadmap continues to face delays and supply shortages, while the transition toward Arm-based host processors has proved less disruptive than previously anticipated, Investing.com reported, citing the note. The firm also noted that AMD’s valuation multiple has declined significantly even as earnings estimates have risen. Analysts at William Blair expect AMD's data-center AI revenue to surpass its server central processing unit (CPU) business in the fourth quarter, supported by its Helios AI systems ramping through 2027. It sees the potential for more than 80% revenue growth next year, over twice its longer-term model. AMD and Broadcom (AVGO) gained as investors considered whether Nvidia customers might diversify their chip suppliers. Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu told Bloomberg, “AMD as a direct competitor, and Alphabet and Broadcom in the TPU space, are natural beneficiaries in the short term.” Meanwhile, a Barron’s report cited Pepperstone analyst Chris Weston, who said markets appeared to distinguish between Nvidia-specific risks and the broader AI trade, suggesting investors were not treating Huang's situation as a fundamental threat to AI demand. BofA raised its AMD price target to $700 from $650, maintaining a ‘Buy’ rating, according to TheFly. The firm reiterated AMD as its top central processing unit (CPU) pick, citing its broad product portfolio, leadership across key segments, Zen 6 execution on 2-nanometer technology and improving supply visibility. AMD’s fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 45% year-over-year to $13.4 billion, while data-center revenue surged 97% to $8.5 billion, driven by strong sales of EPYC processors and Instinct graphics processing units (GPUs). Management expects fourth-quarter revenue of around $17 billion, implying 66% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. William Blair nevertheless flagged competition from custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), particularly at Meta Platforms (META) and OpenAI, as a risk to AMD's Instinct business. However, the firm sees these custom chip programs creating additional opportunities for AMD's server CPUs, per the Investing.com report. On Stocktwits, retail investors’ sentiment around AMD stock remained in the ‘extremely bullish’ territory amid high user message volume. So far this year, AMD's share price has more than doubled, surging by over 147%. In comparison, the Invesco NASDAQ 100 ETF (QQQM) and the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), which hold the stock, have risen 12% and 21%, respectively, over the same period. title: ‘A dark day for Nvidia’: Here’s what analysts have been saying about Jensen Huang’s departure - CNBC
content:
Nvidia investors are preparing for a future without Jensen Huang after the CEO’s resignation was announced on Thursday. Markets were on tenterhooks ahead of the decision amid reports that the chip giant’s board had convened to discuss his future with the company. By the time of the announcement, at least six analysts had downgraded the stock between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had engaged in a second extramarital affair with an employee. The CEO was already under scrutiny after Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. Nvidia announced on Thursday morning that, following a board meeting, Huang would step down after more than 30 years at the company’s helm. Those downgrading the stock included longtime Nvidia bull Ben Reitzes of Melius Research. Nvidia shares were seen down more than 12% shortly after the open on Wall Street, bringing losses for the last month close to 25%. Here’s what analysts and investors are saying about the company and the stock. Please contact cnbc support to provide details about what went wrong Reitzes changed his rating for Nvidia to hold from buy. His price target is now $185 — down from $315 — is 6% above the level at which shares last closed. “We thought we had experience, but nothing prepares you for what has happened at Nvidia over the last few weeks - and especially since Saturday. The only situation remotely close to this we can recall was HP in 2010. Waiting to see what that Board would do (and who they would hire) that time didn’t work out. It was really cheap, too, at ~9x EPS right after its initial swoon. Nvidia is a much stronger, more important company, but its market moves far faster, and this story touches geopolitical flashpoints. In this unique crisis, we have decided (reluctantly) to step aside on Nvidia (now a Hold) after recommending it since we launched our AI platform coverage universe in July 2023,” he said. Analyst Mark Lipacis downgraded Nvidia to in line from outperform. He also lowered his price target on shares to $186 from $465, implying 7% upside from Wednesday’s close. “The Wall Street Journal reported Nvidia’s Board was ‘preparing to oust’ its CEO after he had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. The NY Times reported that Nvidia’s Board hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead an investigation into the matter. While Nvidia’s Board said that it ‘has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,’ we believe that the investigation will take time and we expect NVDA’s P/E multiple will continue to compress consistent with our ‘Late-Innings of the Semi Cycle’ thesis, especially since Nvidia has no obvious succession plan or number 2 operational executive,” he said. William Blair’s Sebastien Naji downgraded Nvidia to market perform from outperform. “After a head-spinning week of news and allegations around CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s board is reportedly preparing to remove him, according to the Wall Street Journal. The full story will take time to emerge and may require several investigations, including the board’s own independent probe and a requested U.S. House briefing. What is already clear is that Huang’s likely departure and heightened scrutiny of the company will be a significant overhang on NVDA shares in the near term. Meanwhile, the potential for a slower AI buildout and more intense competition from other chipmakers will only add to execution risk...governance and regulatory pressure, the potential for more serious fallout, and a sudden change in management are likely to muddle both execution and sentiment. As a result, we are downgrading NVDA to Market Perform and will wait for the dust to settle before reassessing,” he said. Analyst Rick Schafer downgraded the AI stock to perform from outperform. “We are downgrading shares of NVDA and removing our price target following reports (WSJ, NYT) of founding CEO Jensen Huang’s imminent departure amidst allegations of a 2nd extramarital affair. Credible media reports circulated Wednesday evening that NVDA’s board is preparing to part ways with Huang following a widely reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy compounded by new allegations of a relationship with an NVDA executive. This ‘one-two’ punch appears to have forced the board’s hand...While we see upside to the F3Q (Oct.) print and F4Q (Jan.) outlook, we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term. The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang,” he said. Analyst Stacy Rasgon slashed his price target from $400 and downgraded the stock from market outperform. “So now what? On the positive, the fundamentals of the business (if not the leadership) areclearly still intact with numbers that remain massive (and probably still headed higher). We don’t think the company should have huge issues operating while engaged in a search for new leadership. And (of course) the shares are almost absurdly cheap (and getting cheaper as we speak); clearly there is a lot of bad news getting priced in here,” he said. “On the other hand, we find it hard to advocate stepping in here in size as there will no doubt be more allegations to come (there is a trope that says if you find two ants in your kitchen the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two...), both from internal issues as well as headlines related to the business, new governmental investigations etc. Adding on the new variable of who will take the reins (internal? external?) and anything else they may or may not uncover creates additional uncertainty (and we can’t even begin to speculate as to who they might find to fill Jensen’s shoes),” he added. Analyst John Vinh downgraded the stock from overweight. “We believe Huang’s departure represents a material increase in strategic, organizational, and execution risk that warrants a higher risk premium and lower valuation multiple for the stock. While we expect core fundamentals to remain strong for the foreseeable future, we believe it will be challenging for NVDA to find a successor with the same leadership and strategic vision as Huang,” he said. “In our view the writing is on the wall that Jensen’s days at Nvidia could be numbered and we would expect this to be a very fluid situation over the next 48 hours,” renowned tech bull Dan Ives said in a note overnight. “Jensen has created a black eye moment for himself and Nvidia and now has created a spider web of complexity that Wall Street, Silicon Valley, DC, and the global tech ecosystem are trying to figure out what is next.” “We believe Nvidia’s value is $300 per share with Jensen as CEO and $225 per share without Jensen as CEO,” Ives added. “The stock will clearly be under pressure with this fluid news but the reality is its a dark day for Nvidia, but the company will navigate this turmoil and get through to the other side and remain a core foundational piece of the AI Revolution.” Citi analysts said overnight that they had trimmed their target price for Nvidia to $225, down from $285. “If Jensen were forced out, it would mark the end of an era,” Malik and Sylla said in their note. “Under his leadership, Nvidia became the dominant force in AI infrastructure, the primary beneficiary of the global AI spending cycle, and one of the world’s most valuable companies. A leadership transition creates an overhang on the stock given his central role in strategy, product vision, customer relationships, and investor confidence.” They said Nvidia CFO Colette Kress could serve as interim CEO while the board evaluates external candidates. “As much as there is a lesson here for Nvidia around corporate governance, around key man risk… the reality is there is still 40,000 other employees at Nvidia, and there is some real talent there, and I have no doubt that there are some executors within Nvidia that the board will be able to tap to execute on their existing plans and continue to manage the company,” Nathan Thooft, the firm’s CIO, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” on Thursday. “I think the bigger risk is the foresight in the next several years, where Nvidia was driven by a lot of the mindset and thoughts that come out of their CEO, and if he’s no longer there they’re going to have to find that replacement.” “You can’t deny the board has done a horrible job of succession planning,” Greifeld told CNBC’s “Morning Call” on Thursday. “What the board has to find out in the next days or weeks is, did Jensen lie to them? Right? Did he lie to them repeatedly on different topics? We don’t know. Does he lose their trust basically on lying to them over the years? I’m sure the board would love to keep Jensen in place in some role. Right, his value to the company is quite large.” Greifeld said he does not see a premium in Nvidia stock, noting that it trades at a low multiple “so there’s no bubble to burst here with respect to the valuation.” “If there’s a new CEO in, they don’t have to make any decisions day one, day 30, day 60. They have time to really get their footing and come up with their own strategic vision,” he told CNBC. “You’re not going to change what is in the development plan for chips that exists today. So I think certainly it would be a loss, but given the nature of the business and the long lead time for these chip developments and the long contractual relationships they have with customers, it would give them certainly room to maneuver.” CIO Richard Reyle told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” that Nvidia’s board had painted themselves into a corner by not having any kind of succession plan in place. “I’ve heard him compared to Steve Jobs being removed from Apple, but [Jobs] put in place a succession plan and cultivated and groomed Tim Cook for years, so that when he passed away and [Cook] took over, there was a real leader there,” he said. “Right now, Nvidia doesn’t have that person in place, so it’s going to be a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with … all kinds of interrogations, or they’re going to have to move on from him, and that’s just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn’t make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable.” Reyle said he saw the stock moving “lower and much lower from here.” “There’s no obvious [replacement] there that can step right in and take over, so they may kind of try to ride this out and retain him,” he said. “But there’s going to be a lot of difficulty in doing so because he’s going to become something of a liability.” “NVIDIA upheaval puts tech concentration risks in focus,” Mark Haefele, global wealth management chief investment officer at UBS, and his team said on Thursday morning. “Without taking any views on individual companies, the episode reinforces the importance of investment diversification and selectivity as the AI trade matures. We retain our conviction in AI’s long-term potential, with compute demand remaining robust and earnings resilient. But elevated expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes can leave concentrated portfolios exposed to company-specific setbacks.” “Jensen Huang is toast,” Bill Blain, founder and principal, said in his morning newsletter. “Nvidia’s dependence on Jensen Huang is now exposed as a major market risk. The dominant firm within the AI industry lacks clear succession planning and Huang was seen as the acceptable face of AI by the public.” “Confidence in the AI sector has been wobbling for months,” he added. “Huang’s departure could lead to instability and trigger another collapse.” Got a confidential news tip? title: Nvidia stock closes down over 4% after CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation - CNBC
content:
Follow CNBC’s live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation here. Nvidia shares declined 4.34% Thursday after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker. The stock hovered under $4 trillion in market cap for most of the day, but climbed slightly heading into the close to finish above the number. The 4% fall pared steeper losses earlier in the day of as much as 14%. Nvidia has closed above the $4 trillion market cap benchmark since July 2025. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed, Nvidia said in a Thursday statement. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China. Alice Huang is also tied to Nvidia’s biggest competitor in China, Huawei, and may have owned stakes in Chinese businesses benefitting Huawei while simultaneously doing business with Nvidia, CNBC’s Eamon Javers exclusively reported Thursday. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell reports to Huang, according to the Times. Huang also had an “intimate relationship” with an unnamed second employee, Reuters reported Thursday. Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that this departure could lead the stock to fall 20%, given how critical he has been to Nvidia’s success. Nvidia’s stock is already down more than 20% over the last month. Bernstein on Thursday slashed its price target on Nvidia’s stock by half from $400 to $200. Stacy Rasgon, a senior analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” on Thursday that Huang’s alleged affair with a direct report means it is “much tougher for the board to leave him in position.” Huang was central to Nvidia’s rise, having co-founded the company in 1993 and was pivotal in transforming Nvidia from a gaming hardware player to the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Rasgon said it is unclear who could be the “visionary” to lead Nvidia into the future as new CEO. “Jensen is Nvidia, right? He is the visionary. The reason they’re in the position that they’re in today is because he made decisions 10 years ago,” Rasgon said. “Who is the right person now to make the decisions for the next 10 years? I don’t intuitively know who that person would be.” Earlier, U.S. lawmakers had called for Huang’s resignation, adding further pressure to the CEO and the company. Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, said Nvidia’s lack of a succession plan makes the stock “uninvestable.” “Nvidia doesn’t have that person in place, and so it’s going to be either a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with months and months of being hauled in front of probably congressional boards and things to explain themselves and all kinds of interrogations,” Reyle told CNBC’s “Access Middle East.” “Or they’re going to have to move on from him, and that’s just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn’t make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable.” Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. As well, a protection racket loses its black-jacketed enforcer," he said. "The coercion, it seems, came from the top." He also questioned whether CFO Colette Kress, a possible interim successor, could fill Huang's role. "I do not see Colette or any new CEO replacing the Don seamlessly," he said. Burry argued that replacing Huang would also mean replacing his influence over customers. "The Don was the Enforcer. NVIDIA is losing both." The investor said the leadership uncertainty added to his concerns about Nvidia's financing and sales practices. "The key-man risk at NVIDIA always was a worry," he said. "If only that were all." Burry warned that Nvidia's investments in companies that buy its chips could leave sales vulnerable if funding slows. "The terms of trade and the architecture of financing were the secret sauce that supercharged an already-dominant technology," he said. Nvidia purchased $42.4 billion in equity securities in the six months ended July 26. In August, it announced preliminary partnerships with six financial groups, including Apollo and BlackRock, aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure over time. Burry pointed to heavy borrowing across the system. "There is tremendous leverage through the system - I have found upwards of 76x," he said.
